research_question: What tools does technical analysis for stocks use, and what does published research say about simple technical rules?

research_brief.purpose: Explain core tools and summarize verifiable research on rule performance.
research_brief.data_period: Studies cover 1897 to 2011 (DJIA) and 1988 to 2011 (S&P 500); CFA reading 2026.
research_brief.scope_limitations: Older peer-reviewed evidence; owner-cited SSRN 6977700 could not be verified and was excluded.

sources.title: Equity Valuation: Concepts and Basic Tools
sources.verification_note: Quoted definition of technical and fundamental analysis confirmed.

sources.title: Breaking Into the Blackbox: Trend Following, Stop Losses and the Frequency of Trading
sources.publisher: Clare, Seaton, Smith, Thomas (Journal of Asset Management)
sources.scope: S&P 500 trend rules, July 1988 to June 2011
sources.method: Backtest with 20 bp cost per trade
sources.verification_note: 200-day monthly 10.66%, Sharpe 0.58 vs buy-and-hold 9.49%, 0.31; volatility one-half to one-third; stop losses add no value confirmed from accepted version.

sources.title: Technical Trading Revisited: False Discoveries, Persistence Tests, and Transaction Costs
sources.verification_note: Abstract confirmed from full PDF: rules not selectable ex ante; performance offset by low transaction costs.

sources.title: Moving Average Strategy Effectiveness Across P/E Ratio Regimes
sources.limitations: Small sample; unreviewed; SSRN blocked direct fetch
sources.verification_note: Title, author, sample, and small effect sizes confirmed via SSRN listing in search results.

statistics.claim: A monthly 200-day moving-average rule on the S&P 500 returned 10.66% a year with a Sharpe ratio of 0.58, versus 9.49% and 0.31 for buy-and-hold, July 1988 to June 2011, with a 20 bp cost per trade.

content_gaps: Ranking pages explain tools but cite no research on whether rules work.
Few discuss transaction costs or data mining.
None separates risk definition from prediction.
value_add: Verified study figures (Clare et al. 2013; Bajgrowicz and Scaillet), cost and data-mining caveats, and a risk-planning section.

claims.statement: Technical analysis uses stock price and trading volume as the basis for investment decisions.
In DJIA data from 1897 to 2011, low transaction costs fully offset in-sample technical rule performance.
